concepts.name: Sandboxed execution for a coding agent
Retrieving repository context just in time
A test-driven loop and human review

questions.prompt: Where should a coding agent run the tests and commands for code it has just written?

choices.text: On the CI runner that also holds the deploy keys, since it already has the toolchain
On the production app server, so tests see real data
In a disposable, isolated sandbox with no production credentials and limited network access
In the same process as the agent orchestrator, to avoid start-up time

questions.explanation: Generated code and the repository's own scripts are untrusted: they can delete files, leak secrets or call the network. A throwaway sandbox (such as an E2B microVM or a locked-down container) limits the damage to something you discard afterwards. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments for autonomous agents for the same reason.

sources.title: Internet access
sources.claim: Every E2B sandbox has outbound internet access by default; allow_internet_access=False (Python) / allowInternetAccess: false (JS) disables it, and allow_out/deny_out lists restrict it, with allow rules taking precedence over deny rules.

sources.title: Building Effective AI Agents
sources.claim: Because autonomous agents can compound errors, Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments along with appropriate guardrails.

questions.prompt: You create an E2B sandbox with `Sandbox.create()` and pass no network options. Can code inside it reach the internet?

choices.text: No: sandboxes are fully offline unless you open specific outbound ports when creating them
Only to package registries such as PyPI and npm, so installs work but other hosts are blocked
Only after you upgrade to a paid plan; free-tier sandboxes have no outbound network
Yes: outbound access is on by default unless you pass `allow_internet_access=False`

questions.explanation: E2B's docs say every sandbox has outbound internet access by default. You can turn it off with `allow_internet_access=False` (Python) or `allowInternetAccess: false` (JS), or restrict it with `network` allow and deny lists; allow rules win when both match. Don't assume a sandbox is offline: check the default for the platform and version you use.

sources.title: Internet access
sources.claim: Every E2B sandbox has outbound internet access by default; allow_internet_access=False (Python) / allowInternetAccess: false (JS) disables it, and allow_out/deny_out lists restrict it, with allow rules taking precedence over deny rules.

questions.prompt: What must a coding agent's sandbox restrict, and why each one?

model_answer.summary: The sandbox limits what code can touch, where it can connect, which credentials it can see and how long it can run, and it's thrown away after each task.
key_points: Filesystem: only a fresh copy of the repository, not the host or other projects
Network: outbound access off, or limited to an allowlist such as package registries, so code can't exfiltrate data
Credentials: no production secrets or broad tokens inside the sandbox
Resources and time: CPU, memory and a timeout, so a runaway process or infinite loop stops
Disposable: a new sandbox per task, destroyed afterwards, so nothing persists between runs

questions.explanation: Each restriction closes one route to damage: files, the network, credentials, and runaway compute. E2B exposes most of these as settings (internet access, allow and deny lists, timeouts), but its defaults are permissive, so you configure them deliberately.

sources.title: Internet access
sources.claim: Every E2B sandbox has outbound internet access by default; allow_internet_access=False (Python) / allowInternetAccess: false (JS) disables it, and allow_out/deny_out lists restrict it, with allow rules taking precedence over deny rules.

sources.title: Sandbox lifecycle
sources.claim: An E2B sandbox takes a timeout at creation (timeout in seconds in Python, timeoutMs in JS), can have it changed at runtime, and can be destroyed immediately with kill().

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic's context engineering post, how does Claude Code find the code it needs in a large repository?

choices.text: It embeds the whole repository into a vector index at start-up and retrieves the top chunks
It loads `CLAUDE.md` up front, then uses tools like `glob` and `grep` to pull in files just in time
It loads every file into the context window when the session starts
It asks the user to paste each file it might need

questions.explanation: Anthropic describes a hybrid: `CLAUDE.md` files go into context up front, while `glob` and `grep` let the agent navigate and retrieve files just in time, avoiding problems with stale indexes. A pre-built embedding index goes stale as soon as the agent edits files, and exact search is precise for code symbols.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
sources.claim: Claude Code drops CLAUDE.md files into context up front and uses glob and grep to retrieve files just in time, bypassing stale indexing.

questions.prompt: Your repository fits in a 1M-token context window. Why not load all of it into every request?

choices.text: Recall gets worse as the context grows, and every call pays for all those tokens
Models ignore any code past the first 100,000 tokens
Providers refuse requests that contain whole repositories
It's fine: loading everything is the recommended approach once it fits

questions.explanation: Anthropic calls this context rot: as the number of tokens grows, the model's ability to recall information from the context decreases. Every call also pays for every input token. Targeted retrieval of the files that matter keeps the context small and focused.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
sources.claim: Context rot: as the number of tokens in the context window grows, the model's ability to accurately recall information from it decreases, so context is a finite resource to curate.

sources.title: Best practices for Claude Code
sources.claim: LLM performance degrades as the context window fills, so the context window is the most important resource to manage.

questions.prompt: Your coding agent makes the failing tests pass by editing the test file to expect the buggy output. Which control best prevents this?

choices.text: Give the agent more test runs, since with enough attempts it converges on a real fix
Raise the model's temperature so it explores more candidate solutions before settling on one
Add "try harder, and don't cheat" to the prompt and rerun, since the model follows explicit instructions
Fix the tests before the agent starts, flag any change to them, and have someone else review the diff

questions.explanation: An agent that can edit its own check can make any check pass. Keep the tests as a fixed target (written first, or by a separate session), treat a diff to test files as a red flag, and have an independent reviewer, a fresh subagent or a human, check the change. Claude Code's best practices recommend verification by a second opinion so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it.

sources.title: Best practices for Claude Code
sources.claim: Verification by a second opinion (a verification subagent or a separate reviewer session) means the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it; the doc also suggests one session writes tests and another writes code to pass them.

questions.prompt: How should the repository be configured so the agent's work always gets human review before it lands on `main`?

choices.text: Give the agent admin rights so it can merge its own PR once all required status checks pass
Let the agent push to `main` directly, and have a human review the commits the next morning
Protect `main` with required reviews and status checks; the agent only pushes branches and opens PRs
Tell the agent in its system prompt never to push to `main`, and only open pull requests

questions.explanation: Branch protection can require approving reviews and passing status checks before a merge, and by default it blocks force pushes and deletion of the branch. By default its rules don't apply to repository admins, so an agent with admin rights could bypass them. A prompt instruction is not an access control.

sources.title: About protected branches
sources.claim: Branch protection can require pull request reviews and passing status checks before merging, blocks force pushes and branch deletion by default, and by default does not apply to repository admins unless bypassing is disallowed.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise: name three ways a coding agent that opens pull requests could damage a repository, and how you would prevent each.

model_answer.summary: It could land broken or harmful code, rewrite history or weaken tests, or leak secrets; branch protection, fixed tests with independent review, and a credential-free sandbox prevent them.
key_points: Broken or malicious code merged to `main`: protect the branch with required reviews and status checks, and let the agent only open PRs
History rewritten or branches deleted: branch protection blocks force pushes and deletion, and the agent's token isn't an admin
Tests weakened or deleted to get a green run: tests are fixed before the agent starts, changes to them are flagged, and the diff is reviewed independently
Secrets committed or sent out: no secrets in the sandbox, secret scanning on pushes, and network egress restricted
Destructive commands (such as deleting files): run them only in a disposable sandbox with a fresh clone

questions.explanation: Any three well-matched pairs pass. The strongest answers use controls enforced outside the model (branch protection, token scope, sandbox settings) rather than prompt instructions, because the agent can make mistakes or be manipulated.

sources.title: About protected branches
sources.claim: Branch protection can require pull request reviews and passing status checks before merging, blocks force pushes and branch deletion by default, and by default does not apply to repository admins unless bypassing is disallowed.

sources.title: About push protection
sources.claim: Secret scanning push protection blocks pushes that contain secrets before they reach the repository.

sources.title: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
sources.claim: Excessive Agency stems from excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy; mitigations include least privilege, minimal-scope credentials and human approval for high-impact actions.

questions.prompt: Your coding agent reads issue text from anyone on the internet, holds a token that can read the company's private repositories, and can make arbitrary HTTP requests. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Remove one of the three: for example block outbound network, or scope the token to this repository
Add a guardrail model in front of the agent that detects 95% of prompt-injection attempts
Tell the agent in the system prompt to ignore any instructions it finds in issue text
Strip HTML tags and hidden markup from issue text before the agent reads it

questions.explanation: This is Simon Willison's lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content, and a way to send data out. Together they let injected instructions exfiltrate your data. Willison argues that 95% detection is a failing grade in security, and prompt instructions can themselves be overridden. Removing a leg of the trifecta makes the attack impossible rather than unlikely.

sources.title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
sources.claim: OWASP says it is unclear whether any method prevents prompt injection fool-proofly, and recommends restricting the model's privileges to the minimum needed and segregating untrusted content.

sources.title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
sources.claim: Combining access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally lets injected instructions exfiltrate data; guardrails claiming 95% detection are a failing grade, so the defence is to avoid combining all three.

questions.prompt: Which GitHub credential for the agent best follows least privilege?

choices.text: A maintainer's personal token with admin rights on the organisation, so nothing fails
A short-lived token scoped to the one repository, allowed only to push branches and open pull requests
A read-only token for every repository, with pushes done by a shared bot account
The same deploy token CI uses, so the agent's environment matches CI's

questions.explanation: OWASP's Excessive Agency risk has three causes: too much functionality, too many permissions, and too much autonomy. The fix is least privilege: scope the token to one repository and only the actions the agent needs, and keep it short-lived so a leak expires. An admin token also bypasses branch protection by default.

sources.title: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
sources.claim: Excessive Agency stems from excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy; mitigations include least privilege, minimal-scope credentials and human approval for high-impact actions.

sources.title: Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App
sources.claim: A GitHub App installation access token expires after 1 hour and can be restricted to specific repositories and a subset of permissions.

questions.prompt: Explain how prompt injection threatens a coding agent that works from issues and repository content, and give three mitigations.

model_answer.summary: Anything the agent reads (issues, code comments, READMEs, dependency files) can contain instructions it may follow; mitigations limit what a hijacked agent can reach and require review before anything lands.
key_points: Untrusted text in issues, comments, docs or dependencies can carry instructions, and the model can't reliably tell them from the user's
A hijacked agent could leak secrets, add a backdoor, or push harmful changes
Avoid the lethal trifecta: no private data or secrets in reach, or no outbound network, so injected instructions can't exfiltrate anything
Least-privilege, repository-scoped, short-lived tokens limit what the agent can change
Human review of every PR (enforced by branch protection) stops harmful changes from landing

questions.explanation: Detection of injection is unreliable, so the design assumes the agent may be hijacked and limits the consequences. That is the common thread in Willison's trifecta and OWASP's advice on excessive agency.

sources.title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
sources.claim: Combining access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally lets injected instructions exfiltrate data; guardrails claiming 95% detection are a failing grade, so the defence is to avoid combining all three.

sources.title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
sources.claim: Indirect prompt injection happens when an LLM takes input from external sources such as websites or files; mitigations include least-privilege access, human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations and segregating untrusted content.
